existing_localTerm:
'regional or minority languages'; none holds official status in Lithuanian law
Lithuania is one of five systems promoting them without recognising them
existing_standing: Lithuanian is the sole official language, but steering documents promote regional ones
existing_mediumOfInstruction:
Art 30(2)(2): primary, basic and secondary run bilingually, with Lithuanian
Since the 2020 amendment no pre-school may be run wholly in a minority language
Lithuania's history and geography, world knowledge and civics go in Lithuanian
2023/24: Polish 47 schools, Russian 27, Belarusian 1, German 1; none vocational
Art 30(2): teaching IN the language needs the school statute plus parent demand
existing_taughtAsSubject:
Art 30(2): schools shall create conditions to learn mother tongue, history, culture
Hebrew and Yiddish are taught in general education; Karaim and Romani are not
Art 30(4): a minority member may instead learn it via non-formal education
Lithuanian gets no less time than the mother tongue in those schools, Art 30(2)

existing_localTerm:
'regional or minority languages'; all fourteen hold official status
Poland is one of five EU states with more than 10 such official languages
existing_standing:
Steering documents name every officially recognised language, and only those
Ten or more languages, plus Lemko; each has a core curriculum
Schools must provide one where enough students apply
existing_mediumOfInstruction:
Ratified Art 8.1 a(i), b(i), c(i) — education IN the language, pre-school to secondary
Only Lithuanian is really so taught; Ukrainian has a few schools and a bilingual model
Law makes it request-based, which the Committee of Experts says is not 'make available'
Even if parents asked, there would be no trained teachers and no textbooks, 2023 report
existing_taughtAsSubject:
As-a-subject is the main model for eight languages, generally three hours a week
Seven parental applications open a primary or secondary class, 14 for pre-school in it
Only Polish citizens admitted, and pupils' minority affiliation is checked by auditors
German was cut to one hour in 2022; press reports three hours restored from 2024/25

existing_taughtAsSubject: Not established from the sources consulted. Eurydice's Key Data on Teaching Languages at School in Europe (2023 edition, policy position 2021/22) lists Malta among the countries that neither officially recognise regional or minority languages nor refer to such languages in steering documents issued by top-level education authorities. Maltese and English are both state languages on the same source's Figure A1, so neither is carried on this map as a regional or minority subject.

existing_localTerm:
Both hold official status as 'regional or minority languages', Eurydice Fig. A1
Slovenia is in Eurydice's 'one or two languages' band
existing_standing: Steering documents name every officially recognised language, and only those — one or two
existing_mediumOfInstruction:
Two different tiers: Italian at Art 8.1 level (i), Hungarian only at level (ii)
Italian-medium schooling runs pre-school to vocational in specifically defined areas
Hungarian is a bilingual model, Hungarian and Slovenian meant to be in equal shares
Equal shares often unmet where Hungarian-speaking children are not the majority
existing_taughtAsSubject:
Outside the ethnically mixed areas Hungarian and Italian are offered as foreign languages
Romani is still not taught as a subject in mainstream education
No model exists for teaching Croatian, German or Serbian as minority languages
University taken only at level e(iii): the language studied, not used as a medium
